```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(psych)      
library(ordinal)   
library(readxl)     
library(ggeffects)
library(broom)    
library(gt)    

```

## Question and Predictions

The `bfi` data contain 25 personality items from 2,800 people, five items per Big Five trait. Each item is answered on a 6-point scale from *Very inaccurate* to *Very accurate*.

The **chosen trait is Neuroticism**. The ordered outcome is one Neuroticism item, **N4, "Often feel blue."** The predictor is a person's **Extraversion subscale score**, the mean of E1 to E5 with E1 and E2 reverse-keyed.

I predict that as people are more extroverted, they will be less often to feel blue.

## Load and Inspect the Data

```{r}
#| echo: false

data <- read_excel("./bfi.xlsx")

data<- data|>
  mutate_at(2:26, as.integer)

# Check the data
#head(data)
```

## Data preparation

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

# Labels for the six response options, from lowest to highest
n_levels <- c("Very inaccurate", "Moderately inaccurate", "Slightly inaccurate", "Slightly accurate", "Moderately accurate", "Very accurate")

# Scoring keys with reverse-keyed items
keys <- list(
  Agreeableness     = c("-A1", "A2", "A3", "A4", "A5"),
  Conscientiousness = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "-C4", "-C5"),
  Extraversion      = c("-E1", "-E2", "E3", "E4", "E5"),
  Neuroticism       = c("N1", "N2", "N3", "N4", "N5"),
  Openness          = c("O1", "-O2", "O3", "O4", "-O5")
)

scores<-scoreItems(keys, data, totals = F, min=1, max=6)

scores_df<- scores$scores

# Mutate data to include the ordered outcome, an unordered outcome, and the predictor (raw and centred)
data <- data |>
  select(N4) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(scores_df)) |>
  mutate(
    N4 = factor(N4, levels = 1:6, labels = n_levels, ordered = TRUE),   # The ordered outcome
    highest = factor(names(keys)[max.col(scores_df, ties.method = "first")]),  # Unordered outcome:highest-scoring trait
    extra = Extraversion
  ) |>
  drop_na(N4, extra, highest) |>
  mutate(extra_c = extra - mean(extra))  # Centre AFTER dropping missing cases

extra_bar <- mean(data$extra)
```

# 1. Look at the outcomes first

## The ordered outcome

```{r, n4 counts}
#| echo: FALSE

# Count how many people chose each response option for n4.
n4_counts <- data |>
  count(N4) |>
  # p is the proportion of the sample in each category, P(Y = j).
  mutate(p = n / sum(n))
```

Check that no category is empty or very sparse.

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

n4_counts
```

Every category has plenty of responses (the smallest, *Very accurate*, has `r min(n4_counts$n)`), so each threshold can be estimated without collapsing categories.

This can be displayed graphically:

```{r, n4 bar graph}

#plot the counts
plot_n4 <- ggplot(n4_counts, aes(x = N4, y = n, fill = N4)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(12)) +
  labs(title = "Six ordered categories: 'Often feel blue'",
       x = NULL, y = "People") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
plot_n4
```

## How the predictor relates to the responses

I can also visualize how the predictor relates to the responses, seeing how each person's Extraversion score relates to their N4 response. Because many people have the same Extaoversion score and the same N4 response, I use *`geom_jitter`* to spread out the overlapping points.

```{r, jitter plot}
#| echo: FALSE

plot_jitter<-ggplot(data, aes(extra, as.numeric(N4), colour = N4)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6, labels = n_levels) +
  labs(title = "Higher Extraversion, less often feel blue, with lots of overlap",
       x = "Extraversion (subscale mean, 1-6)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

plot_jitter
```

The outcome takes only six values. A good model should predict a probability for each of those six categories, not a specific decimal average that is not an option to choose.

## An unordered outcome

Each person's **dominant trait** (their highest of the five subscale scores) is a set of categories with **no built-in order**. Being highest on Openness is not "more" than being highest on Agreeableness. An outcome like this requires a baseline-category (multinomial) model, such as `nnet::multinom()`, rather than `clm()`.

Here I can see how many people have each trait as their highest.

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

ordered_dat <- data |>
  count(highest) |>
  mutate(highest = fct_reorder(highest, n)) # fct_reorder() sorts the bars by size

#plot the unordered outcome
unordered_plot <- ggplot(ordered_dat, aes(highest, n)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "maroon") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Dominant trait: five categories with no order",
       x = NULL, y = "People") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

unordered_plot
```

# 2. Cumulative probabilities

A cumulative probability is the probability of responding **with a specific response category (*j*)** or lower. With six categories there are five cumulative probabilities to model. This is because I am dealing with cumulative thresholds which I am converting to probabilities. Remember that cumulative thresholds are cumulative — meaning they capture the probability of a participant providing any response option OR one below it (i.e., selecting slightly inaccurate OR moderately inaccurate OR very inaccurate). That is why I have 5 cumulative probabilities and not six – the cumulative probability of the sixth category (very accurate) is 100%.

```{r, cumulative prob table}
#| echo: FALSE

obs_tab <- data |>
  count(N4) |>
  mutate(
    Probability = n / sum(n),
    CumulativeProbability = cumsum(Probability), #cumsum() is a running total, adding each category's proportion to all the ones below it
    #if_else() leaves the top category blank (NA), because P(above) = 0 the
    CumulativeOdds = if_else(CumulativeProbability < 1,
                             CumulativeProbability / (1 - CumulativeProbability), NA_real_),
    Cumulative_Logodds = if_else(CumulativeProbability < 1,
                                 qlogis(CumulativeProbability), NA_real_)   # qlogis() turns a probability into log-odds

  )

# create a clean table with gt
obs_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    N4 = "Category in N4 (j)",
    n = "n",
    Probability = "P(Y = j)",
    CumulativeProbability = "P(Y ≤ j)",
    CumulativeOdds = "Odds of ≤ j",
    Cumulative_Logodds = "Log-odds of ≤ j"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Probability, CumulativeProbability), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(CumulativeOdds, Cumulative_Logodds), decimals = 2) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")

```

Each cumulative probability splits the scale in two, as at or below *j* versus above *j*.This becomes a binary outcome which I can easily model using logit as my link function. The ordinal model does this at every threshold point at once, and the order of the categories is built in.

# 3. The model with a centred predictor

I **centred** Extraversion earlier, so that the thresholds describe a person of average Extraversion (`r extra_bar`), rather than an impossible person scoring 0 on a 1-6 scale. Centring changes the thresholds but **not** the slope.

When reading the `summary()` output, the **thresholds** are the points at which a response moved from one category to the next. **Coefficients** are the **slopes** which represent the effect of Extraversion on the latent logit scale.

```{r, modelling with a centred predictor}
#| echo: FALSE

# Null model: thresholds only, no predictors
null <- clm(N4 ~ 1, data = data)

# One-predictor model
one_pred <- clm(N4 ~ extra_c, data = data)

summary(one_pred)
```

```{r, saving elements for inline code}
#| echo: FALSE


# coef() lists every estimate in the model: the 5 thresholds first, then the slope.
coef(one_pred)

# The slope for Extraversion, pulled out by name
b <- coef(one_pred)[["extra_c"]]

# The five thresholds are the first five estimates
th <- coef(one_pred)[1:5]

# Category probabilities for a person of average Extraversion (extra_c = 0).
# plogis() turns log-odds into a probability, so plogis(th) gives P(Y <= j).
cum_avg <- plogis(th)

# Category probabilities for a person of average Extraversion (extra_c = 0).
# cumulative probabilities. Writing them out one at a time:
cat_p <- c(cum_avg[1] - 0,          # Very inaccurate
           cum_avg[2] - cum_avg[1], # Moderately inaccurate
           cum_avg[3] - cum_avg[2], # Slightly inaccurate
           cum_avg[4] - cum_avg[3], # Slightly accurate
           cum_avg[5] - cum_avg[4], # Moderately accurate
           1 - cum_avg[5])          # Very accurate

# tidy() (broom package) turns the model output into a data frame.
#   conf.int = TRUE      -> add 95% confidence intervals
#   exponentiate = TRUE  -> report odds ratios (e^beta) instead of log-odds
# filter(coef.type == "location") keeps the slope and drops the thresholds.
or_tab <- tidy(one_pred, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  filter(coef.type == "location")
```

The estimated slope is beta = `r b`, so Higher Extraversion **raises** the log-odds of being at or below each threshold, which shifts responses toward the **lower** ("inaccurate") categories.

## What the centred thresholds mean

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

# plogis() turns a log-odds into a probability. 

tibble(
  Category = n_levels,
  theta = c(th, NA),
  cum = c(plogis(th), 1),
  cat_p = diff(c(0, plogis(th), 1))
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    theta = "Threshold above category",
    cum = "P(Y ≤ j)",
    cat_p = "P(Y = j)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = theta, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(cum, cat_p), decimals = 2) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")

```

Apply `plogis()` to each threshold to get a cumulative probability, then take differences. For a person of average Extraversion, the most likely response is *`r n_levels[which.max(cat_p)]`* (`r max(cat_p)`). Their probability of endorsing the item at all, that is, *Slightly accurate* or lower, is the probability of *Slightly accurate* at 79%. 

# 4. Null model versus one-predictor model

The null model has thresholds only. With no predictors, its thresholds reproduce the observed cumulative log-odds from Section 2 exactly:

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

# View thresholds produced, and how they are the same as the cumulative log-odds
coef(null)
obs_tab$Cumulative_Logodds[1:5]
```

This is a useful sanity check: it shows the thresholds are just cumulative log-odds. Once a predictor is added, the thresholds become *conditional* on it (here, describing an average-Extraversion person), so they no longer match the raw proportions.

Now I compare the two nested models with a likelihood ratio test (LRT) and AIC:

```{r, LRT}
#| echo: FALSE

# anova() on two clm models gives an LRT
lrt <- anova(null, one_pred)
lrt
```

Adding Extraversion improves fit substantially.

```{r, AIC}
#| echo: FALSE

# logLik() and AIC() pull the fit statistics from each model.
# length(coef(...)) counts the estimated parameters.
tibble(
  Model = c("Null", "Extraversion"),
  Parameters = c(length(coef(null)), length(coef(one_pred))),
  logLik = c(logLik(null), logLik(one_pred)),
  AIC = c(AIC(null), AIC(one_pred))
) |>
  mutate(`ΔAIC` = AIC - min(AIC)) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(logLik, AIC, `ΔAIC`), decimals = 1)
```

AIC agrees with the likelihood ratio test: the Extraversion model is preferred by a wide margin (ΔAIC = `r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(null) - AIC(one_pred))`).

## 4b. Comparing and interpreting the chosen model

```{r, lrt aic values for inline coding}
#| echo: FALSE

# The LRT table has one row per model; row 2 holds the test results.
# $ pulls out a column by name.
lr_stat <- lrt$LR.stat[2]
lr_df <- lrt$df[2]
lr_p <- lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
d_aic <- AIC(null) - AIC(one_pred)
```

The slope, beta = `r b`, is on the latent logit scale. A one-point increase in Extraversion moves a person's latent "sad proneness" as reflected by N4 down by `r abs(b)`. The middle categories are each about `r mean(diff(th)[2:3])` units wide on that scale, so one point of Extraversion shifts someone by roughly `r 100 * abs(b) / mean(diff(th)[2:3])`% of a category.

# 5. Checking proportional odds

The model assumes one shared slope across all five threshold `nominal_test()` refits the model with a separate Extraversion slope at each threshold and compares the two models with an LRT.

`nominal_test()` checks it by fitting a second model in which Extraversion gets a separate slope at each threshold: a different push at each gap. A likelihood ratio test then compares the two models. If giving Extraversion five pushes doesn’t fit significantly better than one, the shared slope is enough and the proportional odds assumption holds.

```{r, nominal test}
#| echo: FALSE

nt <- nominal_test(one_pred)
nt
```

```{r, nominal values for inline}
#| echo: FALSE

# nt is a table: pick out [row, column] by name

nt_lrt <- nt["extra_c", "LRT"]
nt_df <- nt["extra_c", "Df"]
nt_p <- nt["extra_c", "Pr(>Chi)"]
```

The test is **not** significant. The data are consistent with a single shared slope, so the proportional-odds model is retained.

If this test was significant, I should use a partial proportional-odds model as seen below, and report this alongside the main model.

```{r, nominal fit model}
#| echo: FALSE

#fit this model
m_nom <- clm(N4 ~ 1, nominal = ~ extra_c, data = data)

#compare the two models to see which has superior fit (commented out for now)
#anova(one_pred, m_nom)
```

```{r, nominal coefficients for inline}
#| echo: FALSE

# Look at the estimates: the first 5 are the thresholds,
# and estimates 6 to 10 are the five Extraversion slopes (one per threshold).
coef(m_nom)

# The five threshold-specific slopes
nom_est <- coef(m_nom)[6:10]

# Their standard errors. vcov() gives the variance-covariance matrix of the
# estimates; diag() takes its diagonal (the variances), and sqrt() turns
# variances into standard errors.
nom_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m_nom)))[6:10]

threshold_or <- tibble(
  Threshold = c("Very inaccurate | Moderately inaccurate",
                "Moderately inaccurate | Slightly inaccurate",
                "Slightly inaccurate | Slightly accurate",
                "Slightly accurate | Moderately accurate",
                "Moderately accurate | Very accurate"),
  Estimate = nom_est,
  SE = nom_se,
  OR = exp(-Estimate),              
  low = exp(-(Estimate + 1.96 * SE)),
  high = exp(-(Estimate - 1.96 * SE))
)
```

If my model required nominal effects, I would report the threshold-specific odds ratios and their confidence intervals.

# 6. Interpreting the coefficient by changing odds ratios to probabilities

```{r, interpret odds ratio}
#| echo: false

or_tab <- tidy(one_pred, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  filter(coef.type == "location")
```

**Extraversion:** e\^beta = `r or_tab$estimate`, 95% CI \[`r or_tab$conf.low`, `r or_tab$conf.high`\], p `r or_tab$p.value`. Each one-point increase in Extraversion multiplies the odds of responding **above any threshold** (for example, "Slightly accurate or higher" versus lower) by `r or_tab$estimate`. That is a **`r round(100 * (1 - or_tab$estimate))`% decrease** in those odds.

An odds ratio is not a change in the number of categories, and it is not a ratio of probabilities. The table below translates it into probabilities. It uses the threshold between *Slightly inaccurate* and *Slightly accurate*, so it shows the probability of endorsing the item at all:

```{r, converting the OR to probabilities}
#| echo: FALSE

# I use the threshold between "Slightly inaccurate" and "Slightly accurate",
# which is the 3rd threshold: th[3].
# Because the model used centred Extraversion, we subtract extra_bar
# from each raw score first.
# The model gives log-odds of being AT OR BELOW the threshold:
#   log-odds = threshold - slope * extra_c

# Extraversion = 3
logodds_3 <- th[3] - b * (3 - extra_bar)   # log-odds of at or below
prob_3    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_3)         # plogis() -> probability; 1 - it = P(above)
odds_3    <- prob_3 / (1 - prob_3)         # odds of being above

# Extraversion = 4
logodds_4 <- th[3] - b * (4 - extra_bar)
prob_4    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_4)
odds_4    <- prob_4 / (1 - prob_4)

# Extraversion = 5
logodds_5 <- th[3] - b * (5 - extra_bar)
prob_5    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_5)
odds_5    <- prob_5 / (1 - prob_5)

# Extraversion = 6
logodds_6 <- th[3] - b * (6 - extra_bar)
prob_6    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_6)
odds_6    <- prob_6 / (1 - prob_6)

prob_tab <- tibble(
  Extraversion = c(3, 4, 5, 6),
  Prob = c(prob_3, prob_4, prob_5, prob_6),
  Odds = c(odds_3, odds_4, odds_5, odds_6)
)

prob_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Prob = "P(Slightly accurate or higher)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Prob, Odds), decimals = 2)
```

Each one-point step multiplies the odds by `r prob_tab$Odds[2] / prob_tab$Odds[1]`, which is the OR. The **probability**, however, falls by `r prob_tab$Prob[1] - prob_tab$Prob[2]` from 3 to 4 but by only `r prob_tab$Prob[3] - prob_tab$Prob[4]` from 5 to 6. A constant odds ratio implies different probability changes depending on where you start, which is why I also plot predicted probabilities.

# 7. Predicted probabilities and odds ratios

## 7a. Predicted category probabilities

```{r, pred}
#| echo: FALSE

# ggpredict() returns one row per Extraversion value x response category.
pred <- ggpredict(one_pred, terms = "extra_c [all]")
```

```{r, stacked plot}
#| echo: FALSE

pred |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(
    response.level = factor(response.level,
                            labels = n_levels),
    extra = x + extra_bar   
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(extra, predicted, fill = response.level)) +
  geom_area(position = "stack") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted probability of each response to N4: 'Often feel blue'",
       x = "Extraversion (subscale mean)", 
       y = "Predicted probability", fill = NULL) 
```

At low Extraversion, much of the probability sits in the "accurate" categories. As Extraversion rises, it moves toward *Very inaccurate* and *Moderately inaccurate*. At every value of Extraversion, the six probabilities sum to 1, which is why the stack always reaches 100%.

## 7b. Coefficient plot of cumulative odds ratios

The plot shows the shared proportional-odds OR alongside the threshold-specific ORs from Section 5, so it also works as a visual check of proportional odds.

```{r, OR plot}
#| echo: FALSE

bind_rows(
  tibble(Threshold = "Shared (proportional odds)", OR = or_tab$estimate,
         low = or_tab$conf.low, high = or_tab$conf.high, type = "Shared"),
  threshold_or |> transmute(Threshold, OR, low, high, type = "Threshold-specific")
) |>
  mutate(Threshold = fct_rev(fct_inorder(Threshold))) |>   # keep thresholds in order, top to bottom
  ggplot(aes(OR, Threshold, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +  # OR = 1 means no effect
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative odds ratios per point of Extraversion",
       x = "Odds ratio (responding above the threshold)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Every interval sits well below 1 (the dashed line). The threshold-specific estimates also cluster around the shared estimate, which is what proportional odds implies.

# 8. Results paragraph

I fit a cumulative logit (proportional-odds) model predicting responses to "Often feel blue" from mean-centred Extraversion (N= `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")`). Extraversion improved fit over a null model, chi\^2(`r lr_df`) = `r lr_stat`, p `r lr_p`. As predicted, more extraverted people were less likely to endorse the item, OR = `r or_tab$estimate`, 95% CI \[`r or_tab$conf.low`, `r or_tab$conf.high`\]: each one-point increase in Extraversion lowered the odds of a higher response by about `r round(100 * (1 - or_tab$estimate))`%. The proportional-odds assumption held, chi\^2(`r nt_df`) = `r nt_lrt`, p `r nt_p`. The predicted probability of endorsing the item fell from `r prob_tab$Prob[1]` at an Extraversion score of 3 to `r prob_tab$Prob[4]` at a score of 6 (Figure X).
